title: Autism isn't a line, it's a ten-dimensional spectrum with four genetic clusters
dek: DSM-5 puts Musk and someone who can't dress themselves in the same bucket, but autism has no biomarkers — only four genetic clusters and a pile of misread labels.
why: Medium information density, but the back half — on false positive rates, the double empathy data not holding up, and 10x engineers being autism — lands directly on readers who build products and hire.
who: Founders and product people interested in neurodiversity, the 10x engineer myth in hiring, or the intersection of religion and cognitive style.
skip: The detection algorithm technical details from 1:00:32 to 1:16:51 can be fast-forwarded; the conclusions are in the points.

points.h: The word neurodiversity has already grown too wide
points.body: Jonathan points out that the boundary of neurodivergent depends entirely on who you ask: when Judy Singer coined the term in the 90s it referred only to Asperger's syndrome and other mild neurodevelopmental conditions, but now some people extend it to old age, Alzheimer's, epilepsy, personality disorders. His core criticism: the word gets used as if it were a unified lobbying bloc, yet the interests inside it conflict — changes made for one part of the neurodivergent population may make things worse for another. His analogy is "European": in the US, saying someone is European is informative; in Europe, it's nearly meaningless.

points.h: DSM-5 puts Musk and severe autism in the same cell
points.body: Under DSM-IV there were three categories: PDD-NOS, Asperger's syndrome, autism, plus high functioning autism. Jonathan cites a friend who did 40 years of Asperger's clinical work: give 200 adults and forbid asking about childhood history, and most clinicians can't tell who is which type — the three names actually refer to the same category. DSM-5 merged them into autism spectrum disorder, then split by support needs into level 1/2/3. One motive for the merger was insurance coding: Asperger's was essentially an "unfunded" category in insurance and special education funding, and organizations like ASAN lobbied for it.

points.h: The spectrum is not a 0-to-100 line
points.body: Jonathan says the spectrum is more like a ten-dimensional multi-axis spectrum, with different trait clusters inside it. The SPARK study collects genetic data from diagnosed people and their families; Litman decomposed the autism phenotype and found four genetic clusters, with profound autism (level 3) associated with the most de novo mutations. He stresses that autism has no definitive biomarker, only genetic and environmental risk factors that raise probability — unlike Down syndrome, it can't be confirmed by genetic testing. SYNGAP1 is one of the mutations highly associated with profound autism, but not all profound autism carries this mutation.

points.h: Cognitive dissonance pressure cooker: autistic people blow open earlier
points.body: He sums up his own exit from evangelicalism as a cognitive dissonance pressure cooker: autistic people have a lower tolerance for cognitive dissonance, and the Christian context generates more opportunities for cognitive dissonance, the two stacking into a perfect storm. The techniques religion uses to relieve dissonance weren't designed for autistic people either, so the pressure valve fails. Pressure accumulates until some triggering event — reading something, arguing with someone — and the whole thing collapses. He adds that autistic people tend to bite the bullet, pushing the literal logic of doctrine all the way through, rather than softening it the way most people do.

points.h: 85% of autistic people say they have no personal relationship with Jesus
points.body: After re-converting, Jonathan entered a highly ritualized tradition: prayers are all in books, every service moves to a strict liturgical rhythm. In his research he found the high church drift phenomenon — autistic Christians flowing from low church evangelicalism to high church. In his dataset, asked "do you have a personal relationship with Jesus," 85% answered no; the control group's proportion was almost the reverse. He says that if Christianity had to be practiced in that emotionalized way, he would not have re-converted and would have stayed an atheist.

points.h: Autistic people are easier for cults to capture
points.body: Jonathan says autistic people joining cults happens "very often." The mechanism is a stack of factors: cults specifically hunt people who are socially rejected and marginalized; autistic black-and-white thinking, extreme rigidity, and lack of nuance (one of the DSM criteria) fit cult methods naturally; social difficulty makes them easy to isolate, so the cult says "we are your only family." He also mentions that the charismatic circle has strong anti-mental-health messaging, with some believing autism is demon possession and trying to cast out the "demon of autism," so he usually only reaches these people after they've left the movement.

points.h: The false positive rate has doubled or tripled
points.body: Jonathan's detection algorithm's false positive rate is generally between 5% and 15%, depending on the group. The younger the group, the higher the false positives, because young people use more internet slang and use autistic as an adjective — instead of saying "that person is awkward" they say "that person is so autistic," instead of "I'm a bit awkward" they say "I'm autistic." Since statements like "I'm autistic" carry very high weight in the detection algorithm, they generate a lot of false positives. He says since he started this research in 2014, the false positive rate in younger groups has doubled or tripled, requiring a "Gen Z correction."

points.h: Forty percent of autism content on TikTok is wrong
points.body: Jonathan scraped autism discourse on TikTok and other social platforms, extracted the text and built a classifier to analyze the various claims, finding that at least forty-odd percent is misinformation — for example citing a study that failed to replicate and had a sample size of only five people. Spencer also mentions finding a study with an interesting conclusion in his religion and autism data, then seeing it had only 19 people. Jonathan says vaccines not causing autism is one big category of misinformation, and another is reverse misinformation from autism self-advocates, such as "autistic people are actually good at reading social cues" and "autistic people don't lack empathy, they're hyper-empathetic."

Jonathan says that once autistic people reach a critical mass in an environment, it isn't they who adapt to others — others start imitating them. Silicon Valley is that kind of environment: autistic traits are adaptive here, so they get cultivated, amplified, and then given a high-status label. His own judgment is that "10x engineer means autism." Elon Musk has publicly said he's autistic, and the label got tied to success. But the rewarded traits come as a package — directness, no filter, not caring about existing structure, hyperfocus locked onto writing code — and they arrive together with cognitive rigidity, moral rigidity, and not caring about appearance, even though those aren't adaptive in themselves.
